extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-olympiad students and problem-solvers (high-school and undergraduate contest training)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and solution principles for algebraic and analytic contest problems (inequalities, sums/products, systems, polynomial identities). Focus on transforming expressions, extremal arguments, telescoping, and classical factorization/irreducibility tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write an expression as a sum of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the left-hand side (or entire expression after moving everything to one side) as a sum of squares so nonnegativity is explicit and equality forces each square to be zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move terms to one side, add/subtract constants as needed and complete squares to produce a sum of squares; conclude each square = 0 for equality cases. Examples: summing three equations and expressing as three squares (problems 4 and 6), rewriting polynomial inequalities as sums of squares to deduce variable equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the square (including adding/subtracting constants under radicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add and subtract specific constants (e.g., 1/4) inside expressions or square-roots to allow completing squares and simplify radical expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and remove small constants suggested by the form (e.g., presence of 4 under sqrt suggests adding/subtracting 1/4) so that terms become perfect squares; used to convert awkward expressions to squared forms and isolate variables (see detailed manipulations in first solution of problem 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpoint method for linear-in-each-variable expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the target expression is linear in each variable separately, its extrema on a box/interval are attained when each variable is at an endpoint of its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix all but one variable and view as linear function in the remaining variable; deduce extremum at endpoints and reduce the problem to checking finitely many corner cases (e.g., xi ∈ {0,1} or {p,q}). Examples: many 'Look at the Endpoints' problems (2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpoint method for convex functions (convex-in-one-variable implies extremum at endpoints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the expression, viewed as a function of one variable with others fixed, is convex (or concave), its maximum (or minimum) on a closed interval is attained at an endpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify convexity in any single variable (via second derivative/signs or by representing as sum of convex functions); then reduce to checking endpoints for global extrema. Applied when terms like α/x + βx + γ appear or when f(x)=C1/x^2 + C2/x + C3 + C4 x is convex (examples in 2.2 and 2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use convexity/monotonicity to reduce to boundary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit convexity or monotonicity in variables (or symmetry) to argue maxima/minima occur at extreme values, allowing substitution of boundary values for variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine convexity with symmetry/endpoint method; e.g., if functions are convex in each variable then maximal value occurs when variables are at interval endpoints; check only the finitely many endpoint combinations (used throughout Section 2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping sums and products
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform the summand or multiplicand into a difference (or ratio) of consecutive terms so that partial sums/products collapse to a few boundary terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial-fraction decompositions, recurrence relations, or algebraic identities to write terms as A_k - A_{k+1} (or factorable products) so the series/product telescopes; then evaluate via first and last terms or limit of tail. Many examples in 2.3 (Putnam, Fibonacci, product telescoping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence relations to telescope
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit the recurrence defining a sequence to express expressions (often reciprocals) as telescoping differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive identities like 1/(x_{k}+1) = 1/x_k - 1/x_{k+1} from the recurrence x_{k+1}=x_k^2+x_k, reducing long sums to 1/x_1 - 1/x_{n+1} (see 2.3 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalize denominators / manipulate radicals to telescope
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalize or algebraically transform terms with radicals so neighboring terms cancel in a telescoping pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply numerator and denominator by conjugates or apply identities to turn sqrt-terms into differences of consecutive radicals; used to turn non-obvious sums into telescoping ones (examples in 2.3 problems involving sqrt(n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-fraction decomposition to achieve telescoping
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose rational expressions into simpler fractions whose sums telescope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve for coefficients A,B in representations like (given rational term) = A/(f_k) - B/(f_{k+1}) so that summation collapses; used in Putnam and other telescoping examples (2.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply AM–GM inequality and equality conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the AM–GM inequality to bound sums/products and identify when equality occurs (usually when involved terms are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AM–GM to replace products by sums or vice versa and deduce bounds; check equality cases to characterize extremal solutions (examples in telescoping and inequality problems, e.g., 2.3.9 and elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution/plugging particular/simple values
rubrics_metrics.description: Plugging specific values (often 0 or 1 or small integers) into functional equations or systems to deduce values or force equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test convenient tuples (e.g., m=n=k=0 or 1) to obtain constraints that force the function to take specific values for all arguments (see problem 13 in 2.1). Useful to deduce constants in functional equations or force contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization identities (Sophie Germain, X^4+1, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use well-known algebraic factorizations (Sophie Germain identity, X^4+1 factorizations, sum/difference of powers) to factor expressions and deduce divisibility, primality, or reducibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply identities to split large polynomials into integer-factorable components to show compositeness or factor cancellation in products (many examples in 2.4, including Sophie Germain and X^4+1 arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eisenstein's criterion for irreducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Eisenstein's criterion with a suitable prime p to prove a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over Z[x].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find prime p dividing all coefficients except leading, with p^2 not dividing constant term; conclude irreducibility. Applied to rule out factorizations for small n (2.4 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use similarity/area determinant and convexity for geometric extremal problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Express geometric quantities (e.g., triangle area via 1/2 determinant) as functions of coordinates which are convex/linear in each coordinate; then apply endpoint/convexity arguments to deduce extremizers occur at vertices/corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write area as determinant half; observe convexity in each coordinate; reduce maximizing area inside a square to checking vertices of the square (2.2.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and substitution to reduce variables (assume variables equal when forced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symmetry and inequality/equation structure to argue all variables must be equal (or some equal), reducing a multivariate problem to one-variable equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that any strict inequality in a chain leads to contradiction via monotonicity or cyclic relations (common in systems where f is increasing), then set x=y=z and solve reduced equation (examples in 2.5 problems 1,4,9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign/ordering arguments to eliminate impossible cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze signs or order relations (x>0, x<0, x<y<z etc.) with monotonicity of involved functions to derive contradictions and restrict possible solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotonicity of functions (e.g., f(t)=4t^2/(4t^2+1) strictly increasing) to propagate inequalities and show cyclic contradictions unless equality holds; then find allowed constants (2.5.1, 2.5.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limiting behavior and piecewise-linearity for global nonnegativity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function is piecewise linear with finitely many breakpoints, show nonnegativity by checking values at endpoints and asymptotic behavior; use limits to control tails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that if function tends to +∞ at infinity and is piecewise linear, any negative value must occur at an endpoint of some linear piece; check those endpoints to prove global nonnegativity (2.2.10 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform inequalities into sums of squares or simple nonnegativity statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraically rearrange inequalities so that they reduce to obvious nonnegativity like (a−b)^2 ≥ 0 or sum of such squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate algebra to express inequalities as (a-b)^2 ≥ 0 or as sum of squared differences; this both proves inequality and characterizes equality cases (see many reductions to (a-b)^2 ≥ 0 throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction combined with geometric/linear operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform an operation that reduces problem size while preserving or improving the desired bound, then apply induction on n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define operations on polygons/variables (e.g., moving a vertex along a side while retaining convexity) that turn the instance into a smaller one; prove linearity ensures extremum at extremities and proceed by induction (2.2.13 polygon operation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit algebraic identities to compare factor sizes and deduce distinctness/divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare monotonicity or size of polynomial factors to deduce distinct prime factors, factor cancellations in products, or compositeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After factoring a polynomial into integer polynomials, use inequality/size arguments (each factor >1 and increasing) to deduce compositeness or that factors are distinct (examples in 2.4.8 and 2.4.9).
